Any pre-admission deposit is collected, held and refunded as the Maryland assisted living regulations require and as stated in the agreement. When a resident is discharged or leaves, [AGENCY NAME] issues a final statement and any refund, and returns the resident's property, within 30 calendar days (COMAR 10.07.14.34). For residents funded through the Community Options Waiver, the program charges only the room and board that Maryland Medicaid allows and does not bill the resident for services the waiver pays for (see GOV-06).

definitions.definition: The written contract between the resident and the program that sets out services, rights and charges.
The OHCQ form that describes the program's services, staffing, and charges so prospective residents can compare programs.
The itemized accounting given at discharge showing all charges, payments, deposits and refunds due.

procedures: The Manager completes the OHCQ Uniform Disclosure Statement for the licensed level of care and bed count. It is checked against the actual services, staffing and charges before first use.

The Uniform Disclosure Statement is given free to any person who asks, in person, by mail or by email, on the same business day when possible, and no later than 2 business days after the request. It is included in all marketing materials, including the website and brochures.

When a service changes, the Manager updates the Uniform Disclosure Statement and files the amended statement with OHCQ within 30 calendar days of the change. A copy of the filing is kept in the licensing file.

Before the resident signs, the Manager gives the resident and representative the resident agreement, the Uniform Disclosure Statement, the Resident Bill of Rights, and the complaint procedure, and allows time to read them and to ask questions.

The Manager uses the OHCQ sample resident agreement and fills in the nonfinancial terms (services, rooms, rules, rights and discharge terms) and the financial terms (each fee, what it covers, any deposit, payment due dates and refund terms) specific to the resident.
The Manager explains the agreement in plain language and in the resident's preferred language. See RR-08.
The resident or representative, and the Manager, sign and date the agreement. The resident receives a copy. The original is filed in the resident record.

If a pre-admission deposit is taken, the business office gives a written receipt, holds it as stated in the agreement, and applies or refunds it as the agreement provides. The deposit amount is [DEPOSIT AMOUNT] and the refund terms are written in the agreement.

For a resident funded by the Community Options Waiver, the agreement shows the waiver rate for services and the room and board charge allowed under Medicaid rules, which is currently up to $420 per month. The Manager confirms the current amount with Maryland Medicaid before each new admission. See GOV-06.

The Manager sends written notice of a rate increase to the resident and representative at least 45 calendar days before the increase takes effect. The notice states the new rate, the effective date, and the reason. A copy is filed in the resident record.
A resident who is unhappy with a rate increase may discuss it with the Manager, may use the complaint procedure (RR-02), and may end the agreement (ADM-09).
If services change for a resident, the agreement is amended in writing, signed, and a copy is given to the resident before the change takes effect.

At discharge, the business office prepares a final statement showing all charges, payments, deposits and refunds. It issues the final statement, any refund due, and the resident's property to the resident or representative within 30 calendar days of discharge. See ADM-08.
The business office keeps a copy of the final statement, the refund record and a signed property receipt in the resident record.
The Manager reviews all resident agreements and the Uniform Disclosure Statement at least annually and when the fee schedule or services change, and updates them as needed. See GOV-03.

responsibilities.duty: Completes and updates the Uniform Disclosure Statement, signs agreements, gives rate increase notices, and approves final statements.
Collects and records deposits and payments, prepares final statements, and issues refunds within 30 calendar days.
Give the Uniform Disclosure Statement and agreement to prospective residents and explain them.
Approves the fee schedule and the agreement form.

documentation: Signed resident agreement (nonfinancial and financial terms)
Current and amended Uniform Disclosure Statement and OHCQ filing record
Log of Uniform Disclosure Statement requests and date given
Deposit receipts and refund records
45-day rate increase notices
Final statement, refund and property receipt

policies.title: Resident Funds and Personal Property
policies.applies_to: Residents, business office staff, Manager and all staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect residents' money and belongings by setting strict rules for managing funds, keeping records, and returning property.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] manages a resident's personal funds only on the express written request of the resident or the resident's agent (COMAR 10.07.14.39). Funds of $300 or more are kept in an interest-bearing account. [AGENCY NAME] carries a bond, a letter of credit, or net assets equal to the average monthly balance of resident funds it holds, with the State as obligee. The Attorney General may investigate abuse of residents' funds. [AGENCY NAME] [does / does not] manage residents' funds; the choice is stated in the resident agreement. If [AGENCY NAME] does not manage funds, the agreement says so and procedures 3 to 12 do not apply. Staff may not borrow from, accept gifts from, or take any benefit from a resident's money or property. Resident funds are never mixed with the program's funds. At discharge, [AGENCY NAME] returns the resident's property and any funds within 30 calendar days (COMAR 10.07.14.34).

definitions.definition: Money belonging to the resident that is held or managed by the program on the resident's written request.
A person legally authorized to act for the resident in financial matters, such as under a power of attorney.
The party protected by the bond or letter of credit, which in Maryland is the State.

procedures: The Governing Body decides whether [AGENCY NAME] will manage resident funds. The decision is written in the resident agreement.

If [AGENCY NAME] does not manage funds, the Manager tells each resident and representative at admission, in the agreement, that the program will not hold or manage their money. Residents and families make their own arrangements.

A resident or agent who wants the program to manage funds signs a written request on the Resident Funds Authorization form before any money is accepted. The request states the scope, the amount, and the date. The Manager keeps the original in the resident record.
No staff member may ask a resident to request fund management, and a resident may withdraw the request in writing at any time.
The business office gives a written, numbered receipt every time money is deposited, and records it in a separate ledger for each resident.
Each resident's funds are kept separate from the program's operating funds. Funds of $300 or more are placed in an interest-bearing account. The interest belongs to the resident.

The business office keeps the bond, letter of credit or proof of net assets that equals the average monthly balance of resident funds, with the State as obligee. The business office reviews the amount every quarter and increases coverage when the average balance rises.

The business office releases funds to the resident or agent on request, within 1 business day for amounts held as petty cash and within 3 business days for other amounts. Each withdrawal is recorded and signed for by the resident or agent.
Purchases for a resident are made only with the resident's or agent's approval. Receipts are kept and attached to the ledger.
The business office gives each resident or agent a written statement of the account at least quarterly, and whenever asked, and keeps a copy.
The Manager reviews and signs the ledgers monthly. A person other than the one who keeps the ledger reconciles the account to bank statements monthly. Differences are explained in writing.

Staff must report any suspected missing or misused funds to the Manager immediately. The Manager investigates and, if exploitation is suspected, follows SAF-01 including 24-hour reports. The Attorney General may investigate abuse of resident funds, and the program cooperates fully.
Staff may not accept loans, gifts or gratuities from residents, use residents' property, or act as a resident's agent for finances. See STF-06.
At admission, staff list the resident's personal property on an inventory form signed by the resident or representative. The inventory is updated when items are added or removed.
Staff take reasonable care of residents' property. If an item is lost or damaged, staff report it to the Manager the same day, and the Manager investigates and documents it.

At discharge or death, the Manager returns property and funds, with the final statement, to the resident or the person lawfully entitled within 30 calendar days. The recipient signs a property and funds receipt. See ADM-08 and HLT-09.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether the program manages resident funds and makes sure the bond, letter of credit or net assets requirement is met.
Reviews ledgers monthly, investigates missing funds or property, and makes sure funds and property are returned within 30 calendar days.
Keeps separate ledgers, issues receipts and statements, maintains the interest-bearing account and bond, and reconciles monthly.
Protect residents' property, never borrow or accept gifts, and report suspected misuse immediately.

documentation: Resident Funds Authorization form (written request)
Resident ledger and numbered receipts
Interest-bearing account statements and monthly reconciliation
Bond, letter of credit or net asset documentation naming the State as obligee
Quarterly resident account statements
Personal property inventory and discharge property and funds receipt
Incident reports for missing funds or property

policies.title: Advance Directives and Resident Preferences
policies.applies_to: All residents and representatives; the Manager, Delegating Nurse, and all direct care staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident's advance directive and care preferences are asked about, recorded, easy to find in an emergency, and followed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] asks every resident, at admission, whether the resident has an advance directive, and files a copy of any directive in the resident record. Admission does not depend on a resident having or not having a directive. The resident's preferences about care, daily routine and end-of-life wishes are recorded in the service plan, consistent with the resident's rights (COMAR 10.07.14.36). Staff are trained to find the advance directive at once in an emergency. The directive and the emergency data sheet go with the resident on any acute transfer (COMAR 10.07.14.34). The directive is reviewed again after a hospital stay, because the Delegating Nurse reassesses the resident within 48 hours of readmission (COMAR 10.07.14.29). The resident may change or withdraw a directive at any time, and the record is then updated.

definitions.definition: A written statement of a resident's wishes about medical treatment, or the appointment of a health care agent, made in advance of a time when the resident cannot decide. It includes a living will and a health care power of attorney.
Physician or nurse practitioner orders about life-sustaining treatment, such as a MOLST form, that staff and emergency responders follow.
A summary of the resident's identification, diagnoses, medications, allergies, contacts and directive status that goes with the resident on an acute transfer.

procedures: During pre-admission screening and admission, the Manager or Delegating Nurse asks the resident, in plain language, whether the resident has an advance directive, a health care agent, or medical orders such as a MOLST, and records the answer on the Admission Checklist.
If the resident has any of these documents, staff ask for a copy and file it in the front section of the resident record, where it can be found quickly. Staff also record where the original is kept.

If the resident does not have a directive, the Delegating Nurse offers information and tells the resident they may complete one with their physician, attorney or other advisor. The program does not require a directive and does not complete one for the resident.
Staff record the health care agent's name and phone number on the face sheet and the emergency data sheet.

The Delegating Nurse and the resident record the resident's care preferences in the service plan. These cover daily routine, meals, activities, privacy, spiritual wishes, who to call, and end-of-life wishes. See ADM-04 and REC-02.
A resident with cognitive impairment is asked about preferences as far as possible, and the representative or family adds what they know of the resident's wishes.
The Manager checks that every resident record has the directive status recorded within 7 days of admission. Any missing item is followed up and noted.
At orientation and annually, all staff are trained on where directives are kept, how to find them in an emergency, and how to follow them. Training attendance is documented.

In an emergency, the staff on duty retrieve the directive and medical orders, show them to emergency responders, and follow them as the law and the order provide. Staff call 911 unless a valid order says otherwise.

On acute transfer, staff send the emergency data sheet, a copy of the directive and any medical orders with the resident, and record in the resident record what was sent and when. See HLT-04 and ADM-07.

When a resident returns from a hospital stay, the Delegating Nurse reassesses the resident within 48 hours of readmission and reviews whether the directive and medical orders have changed. The record is updated with any new documents.
A resident may change or revoke a directive at any time. Staff file the new document, remove or mark the older one as superseded, and tell all shifts at the next handoff.

The Delegating Nurse reviews each resident's directive and preferences at every reassessment and whenever there is a significant change in condition. The service plan is updated if wishes have changed. See ADM-03.

When a resident has a health care agent, staff include the agent in discussions of care and notify the agent of significant changes in the resident's condition, as the resident permits and the law allows.
If staff have a question about whether a directive applies, they call the Delegating Nurse or the resident's physician and document what they were told.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure directive status is asked about and recorded, and that staff are trained.
Discusses directives with residents, files documents, reviews them at reassessment and after readmission, and updates the service plan.
Know where directives are kept, retrieve them in an emergency, send them with the resident on transfer, and report changes in the resident's wishes.
Provide a copy of any directive and tell staff when wishes change.

documentation: Admission Checklist showing advance directive inquiry
Copy of advance directive, health care agent designation and medical orders in the resident record
Service plan preferences section
Emergency data sheet and record of documents sent on transfer
Readmission reassessment note (within 48 hours)
Staff training attendance records

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers, students, delegating nurses, residents and resident representatives of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy and confidentiality of resident information in every form (paper, electronic, verbal, photographic). To make sure records are released, secured, retained and destroyed only as the law permits.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps all resident information confidential. Confidentiality is a right in the Resident Bill of Rights (COMAR 10.07.14.36) and is described in RR-01. Resident records are released, retained and disposed of only as permitted by Maryland Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3 (Maryland Confidentiality of Medical Records Act), as cross-referenced in COMAR 10.07.14.29. Records are kept for 5 years after discharge. Whether or not [AGENCY NAME] is a covered entity under HIPAA, it adopts the privacy and security standards of 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164 as its operating standard. [PRIVACY OFFICER NAME], designated in writing by the governing body, is the Privacy Officer. Staff may use or disclose only the minimum information necessary for their job duties. Resident records are kept locked or access-controlled at all times. Any suspected breach is reported immediately and handled under the breach-response process below.

definitions.definition: Any identifiable information about a resident's health, care, services or payment, in any form, including the resident record, medication records, photographs and conversations.
The least amount of PHI needed for a staff member to do a specific task or for a specific permitted disclosure.
The person the resident has authorized, or who is legally authorized, to act for the resident. Disclosure is limited to the scope of that authority (see RR-01).
An unauthorized access, use or disclosure of PHI that compromises its privacy or security, whether accidental or intentional.
A written, signed, dated permission from the resident or representative to release PHI for a stated purpose to a named person or organization.

procedures: The governing body designates the Privacy Officer in writing at licensure and whenever the role changes. The designation is filed in the policy manual and posted in the staff area.

The Privacy Officer gives each new employee, contractor, volunteer and student privacy training before they have access to any resident information (see STF-03). Each person signs a Confidentiality Agreement, which is filed in the personnel record (STF-05). Refresher training is given at least annually and after any breach.

The Privacy Officer assigns each role the categories of PHI it may access (minimum necessary), for example direct care staff, certified medication technicians, delegating nurse, manager and billing staff. The role-access list is reviewed every 6 months.

Active resident records are stored in a locked cabinet or locked room, or in a password-protected electronic system with a unique login for each user. Records are never left unattended on counters, carts or desks. Staff log out of screens when they leave a workstation.

At admission the manager gives the resident and representative a Notice of Privacy Practices written in plain language. The manager explains how information is used, who may see it and how to request access, an amendment or an accounting of disclosures. Receipt is documented in the resident record.

Routine use and disclosure for treatment, care coordination and payment (for example the physician, delegating nurse, pharmacy, hospice, home health agency, hospital and the Medicaid program) is limited to the minimum necessary. The staff member documents the recipient and purpose when disclosure is outside the care team.

Before releasing any record or PHI for a purpose outside treatment, payment or operations, the Privacy Officer verifies the requester's identity and authority and obtains a signed Authorization, unless Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3 or another law permits release without one. Disclosures are logged on the Release of Information Log.

Disclosures required or permitted by law are made only after the Privacy Officer reviews the request. This includes access by OHCQ surveyors, the Long-Term Care Ombudsman (RR-03), Adult Protective Services and law enforcement. The Privacy Officer records what was released, to whom and on what authority.

Residents and their authorized representatives may inspect and obtain copies of the resident record. The Privacy Officer processes requests promptly and within the time required by Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3 and 45 CFR Part 164. Requests for amendment are reviewed by the Privacy Officer, and the outcome is documented and told to the requester.

Staff do not discuss residents in hallways, dining areas or public spaces, or on personal phones or social media. Staff do not take or post photographs or video of residents without a signed resident or representative consent. Whiteboards, sign-in sheets and posted schedules show only the minimum information needed (for example first name only).

Visitors and other residents are not told about another resident's condition, medications or location beyond what that resident has agreed to. Staff who receive inquiries from callers neither confirm nor deny residency until the resident's wishes are checked.

Faxes, email and text messages containing PHI are sent only through secure methods approved by the Privacy Officer. The sender checks the recipient's number or address before sending. Personal email and unsecured text are not used for PHI.

When a record is no longer needed, it is kept for 5 years after discharge (see REC-01), then destroyed by shredding or secure electronic erasure under Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3. The Privacy Officer records the date, method and the person who carried out destruction on the Record Destruction Log.

Any employee who suspects or discovers a privacy breach (lost chart, misdirected fax, unauthorized access, stolen device) reports it to the Privacy Officer immediately, and no later than the end of the shift. The employee does not attempt to retrieve or delete information on their own.

Within 1 business day the Privacy Officer starts an investigation and takes steps to contain the breach, such as retrieving documents, disabling accounts and changing passwords. The Privacy Officer completes a Breach Risk Assessment form and records the information involved, who received it and the risk of harm.

If the assessment finds a reportable breach, the Privacy Officer notifies the affected resident or representative in writing without unreasonable delay and within the outer time limit of 45 CFR Part 164. The Privacy Officer also makes any notification to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services or other agencies required by law, and the manager reviews the need for any report to OHCQ (see REC-03).
The Privacy Officer applies sanctions under STF-06 to any employee who violates this policy. Sanctions are consistent and documented, with no retaliation against anyone who reports in good faith.

The Privacy Officer reports all privacy incidents and breaches to the governing body and the quality assurance committee at least quarterly (GOV-04), and reviews this policy at least annually (GOV-03).

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers, applicants for admission, residents and resident representatives of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every applicant and resident is treated without discrimination and has meaningful access to information and services. This includes people with disabilities and people with limited English proficiency.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in admission, care, services, room assignment, retention or discharge on the basis of race, color, national origin, sexual orientation, gender identity, religion, physical disability or mental disability, as required by COMAR 10.07.14.23 A. This policy also reflects the Resident Bill of Rights (COMAR 10.07.14.36). It follows the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 USC 12101 et seq.), Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 USC 2000d) and 45 CFR Part 92 to the extent they apply to the program. Admission decisions are based only on the criteria in ADM-01 and ADM-05, which concern the ability of the program to meet the person's care needs within its licensed level of care. They are not based on a protected characteristic. [AGENCY NAME] provides qualified interpreters, translated materials and auxiliary aids at no cost to residents and representatives. It makes reasonable accommodations for residents with disabilities.

definitions.definition: A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English well enough to take part in care and services.

A person who is competent in both languages (including sign language) and in the relevant terminology, is impartial and follows confidentiality. Staff members who have been assessed for language skills may serve as qualified interpreters. Family members and friends do so only if the resident asks, as described below.

Items or services that help people with hearing, vision, speech or manual disabilities communicate. Examples are sign language interpreters, large print, Braille, written materials, amplified phones and assistive technology.

A change in rules, policies, practices or the physical setting that gives a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use the services, unless it would fundamentally alter the program or impose an undue burden.
Race, color, national origin, sexual orientation, gender identity, religion, physical disability or mental disability, as listed in COMAR 10.07.14.23 A.

procedures: The manager posts a Notice of Nondiscrimination in a common-use area and includes it in the admission packet and on the program website. The notice states the protected characteristics, how to request language or disability assistance at no cost, and how to file a complaint with [AGENCY NAME] (see RR-02), with OHCQ at (410) 402-8217 or (800) 492-6005, and with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights.

At the first inquiry, the admissions staff member asks the applicant or representative what language they prefer for speaking and reading, and whether they need any auxiliary aid. The preferred language and any communication need are recorded on the Pre-Admission Screening form and carried into the resident record.

Admission staff apply the written admission criteria in ADM-01 to every applicant in the same way. Any decision not to admit is written with the specific clinical or licensure reason (for example, a need for care that the license does not allow). The manager reviews and signs it. Decisions are never based on a protected characteristic or on payment source alone, except as the Medicaid waiver participation policy (GOV-06) provides.

The manager keeps a list of qualified interpreters and language services, including a telephone or video interpreter service available at all times and sign language interpreter contacts. The list is posted in the office and kept current.

When a resident or representative needs language help, staff use a qualified interpreter or translated material at no charge. Staff do not require a resident to bring or pay for an interpreter. Staff do not rely on another resident or a minor child to interpret. Family or friends interpret only if the resident requests it, and staff then document that the offer of a qualified interpreter was made and declined.

Key documents are made available in the resident's preferred language or in an accessible format, or are explained aloud by a qualified interpreter. These include the Resident Agreement, Uniform Disclosure Statement, Resident Bill of Rights, complaint procedure, service plan and any consent or discharge notice. Staff document the method used and who explained it.

For residents who are deaf or hard of hearing, blind or have low vision, or have a speech or cognitive disability, staff provide the auxiliary aid requested or one that is effective for the resident (for example written notes, large print, reading documents aloud, a sign language interpreter). Staff document the aid on the service plan.

A resident, applicant or representative may ask for a reasonable accommodation at any time, orally or in writing. The manager, with the delegating nurse where care is involved, responds within 5 business days, documents the request, the decision and the reasons, and offers an alternative if the first request cannot be granted.

Accommodations may include changes to room or bed assignment, accessible bathing and toileting, flexible meal or activity times, alternative notice formats, help with forms and policy modifications. Service animals are handled under SAF-09, and a request is not denied without a documented review for a safe alternative.

Residents are free to practice their religion and to observe cultural, dietary and personal traditions. Staff accommodate these through the service plan, the dietary plan (DL-01) and the activity program (DL-02), consistent with the safety of other residents.

Staff address residents by their preferred name and pronouns, honor a resident's gender identity in room and roommate assignment and in personal care, and protect privacy about sexual orientation and gender identity (see RR-07). Staff are not permitted to ask for or share such information unless the resident wants it recorded.

All employees receive training on this policy at orientation and at least annually (STF-03). Training covers nondiscrimination, how to use interpreter services, communication with residents with disabilities and how to report a concern.

Any person who believes discrimination has occurred may file a complaint under RR-02 without fear of retaliation. The manager investigates promptly, records the findings and corrective action and reports the result to the complainant. If the complaint involves the manager, it goes to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or the governing body.

The manager reviews language-access requests, accommodation requests, denials of admission and discrimination complaints at least quarterly and reports them to the quality assurance committee (GOV-04) so that patterns can be addressed.

Advises on accommodations affecting care and ensures that assessments and service plans reflect communication needs.
Treat everyone without discrimination, use qualified interpreters, provide auxiliary aids and report concerns.
May ask for language assistance, auxiliary aids or accommodations and may file a complaint at any time.

policies.title: Pre-Admission Screening and Admission Criteria
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Manager, delegating nurse, admissions staff, applicants and their representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure that each person admitted can be safely and appropriately served within the licensed level of care. To make sure each applicant receives the information needed to make an informed decision before admission.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits only persons whose needs can be met within its licensed level of care (Level 1, 2 or 3) and bed count (COMAR 10.07.14.05 and .04). Every applicant is screened before admission. A Resident Assessment Tool (RAT) on the OHCQ form is completed within the 30 days before admission (COMAR 10.07.14.22). The Uniform Disclosure Statement is given to the applicant and representative before admission (COMAR 10.07.14.10). [AGENCY NAME] does not admit a person who needs more than intermittent nursing care, treatment of a stage 3 or 4 pressure ulcer, ventilator services, skilled monitoring of a fluctuating acute condition, or monitoring of a chronic condition that is not controllable (COMAR 10.07.14.23 B). [AGENCY NAME] does not admit a person who is dangerous or at high risk to self or others in a way the program cannot manage (COMAR 10.07.14.23 C). The hospice exception in COMAR 10.07.14.23 D applies only as provided in that section and in HLT-08. Admission decisions are made without discrimination (RR-08).

definitions.definition: The assessment form required and approved by OHCQ, used before admission, at least every 6 months, and after a significant change (COMAR 10.07.14.02).
Nursing care that is needed on a periodic basis and not on a continuous or ongoing skilled basis. The delegating nurse determines whether a need is intermittent.
Level 1 (low), Level 2 (moderate) or Level 3 (high), as named on the license issued by OHCQ.
The OHCQ-prescribed form that describes the services, fees, policies and level of care of the program.
The registered nurse who has a signed agreement with the program and has completed the Board of Nursing delegating nurse course (COMAR 10.07.14.21).

procedures: Admissions staff record every inquiry on the Inquiry Log. At the first contact they ask about the applicant's care needs, the preferred language and the funding source, and tell the caller that the Uniform Disclosure Statement is available free on request.

Before any screening visit, the manager gives the applicant and representative a copy of the current Uniform Disclosure Statement, the Resident Bill of Rights and the proposed Resident Agreement (RR-04). The date given is recorded on the Pre-Admission Screening form. The same Uniform Disclosure Statement is included in marketing materials.

The manager gathers a current medical history, diagnoses, medication list, physician information, a health care provider's evaluation or orders, and any behavioral health history. The manager obtains the applicant's signed release for this information (RR-07).

The manager or a trained designee meets the applicant, in person where possible, and completes the OHCQ Resident Assessment Tool. The RAT must be completed within the 30 days before the admission date. If admission does not happen in that window, a new RAT is completed.

The manager sends the completed RAT to the delegating nurse. The delegating nurse reviews it, performs or arranges any nursing assessment needed (ADM-03) and gives a written opinion on whether the applicant's nursing needs are intermittent and can be met.

The manager and delegating nurse together compare the applicant's needs to the exclusions in COMAR 10.07.14.23 B and C. They check each one: more than intermittent nursing care, stage 3 or 4 pressure ulcer treatment, ventilator services, skilled monitoring of a fluctuating acute condition, monitoring of an uncontrollable chronic condition, and danger to self or others or high risk the program cannot manage. They record the finding for each item on the Admission Criteria Checklist.

The manager confirms that the applicant's assessed needs fall within the licensed level of care (Level 1, 2 or 3) and that a bed is available within the licensed bed count and room standards (ADM-02). If the needs exceed the licensed level, the applicant is not admitted. The manager helps the applicant find an appropriate setting.

If the applicant is in hospice, the manager and delegating nurse review COMAR 10.07.14.23 D and HLT-08 before any decision and document how the hospice services will be coordinated. The program does not use the hospice exception unless the program can meet the applicant's needs with the hospice team.

The manager reviews staffing (STF-01), the program's ability to meet the applicant's needs, including dementia care needs (HLT-05), medication needs (HLT-01 and HLT-02), and any behavioral risks, before accepting the applicant.

The manager makes the admission decision within 3 business days of receiving all information and signs the Admission Decision Form. If the person is not admitted, the manager gives the reason in writing, based only on the criteria above and not on any protected characteristic (RR-08), and offers referral help.

If the applicant is accepted, the manager reviews the Resident Agreement, rates, deposits, refund terms and services with the applicant and representative and answers questions (RR-04). The applicant or representative signs the agreement and the acknowledgment of receipt of the Uniform Disclosure Statement and the Resident Bill of Rights before or on the day of admission.

For an applicant who will use the Medicaid Community Options Waiver, the manager confirms eligibility, the waiver service authorization and the room-and-board arrangement under GOV-06 before admission.

On the day of admission, the manager confirms that the physician's orders and medication supply are in place, assigns the bed (ADM-02), and starts the resident record (REC-01). The service plan is written within 30 calendar days of admission (ADM-04).
If the resident's condition changes between screening and admission, the manager repeats the screening and the delegating nurse reviews the change before the resident moves in.

The manager files the Inquiry Log entry, RAT, delegating nurse review, Admission Criteria Checklist and decision form in the resident's record, or in a pre-admission file for persons not admitted. The manager reports admission refusals and reasons to the QA committee at least quarterly (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Conducts screening, completes the RAT, applies admission criteria, makes and documents the admission decision, and gives the Uniform Disclosure Statement before admission.
Reviews the RAT, assesses nursing needs and advises in writing whether needs are intermittent and can be met within the licensed level.
Keep the Inquiry Log, provide required documents and record the preferred language and communication needs.
Sets the licensed level and bed count, and makes sure resources support the criteria.

policies.title: Bed and Room Assignment Policy
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Manager, delegating nurse, direct care staff, residents and resident representatives
policies.purpose: To assign beds and rooms in a way that stays within the license, meets the physical standards in the regulations, respects resident choice and protects residents' health, safety and dignity.
policies.policy: This policy meets OHCQ Application for Assisted Living Program License, Step Three - On-Site Survey, item 5(a) — Bed and Room Assignment Policy. [AGENCY NAME] never has more residents than the number of beds on its license, and serves residents only within the licensed level of care (COMAR 10.07.14.04). No more than 2 residents share a room. A single room provides at least 80 square feet of functional space and a double room at least 120 square feet, excluding closets, bathrooms and door swings (COMAR 10.07.14.50). Every resident has a real bed; rollaway beds and cots are not used as resident beds. Each room has a door that latches, window shades or other window coverings, and closet space. The program keeps the common space (35 square feet per bed) and toilet, sink and tub or shower ratios required by COMAR 10.07.14.49–.51: 1 toilet and sink per 4 residents and 1 tub or shower per 8 residents. Room assignment is based on the Resident Assessment Tool, the resident's preference, roommate compatibility and the licensed level. Every assignment and every change is recorded on the Bed and Room Assignment Record. Nonemergency moves within the facility require 5 calendar days' notice and the resident's consent (COMAR 10.07.14.34).

definitions.definition: The usable floor area of a bedroom, measured wall to wall, excluding closets, bathrooms and the area swept by door swings.
The program's log of each resident's bed and room, the date of assignment and the date and reason for every change, kept current by the manager.
The number of beds on the license issued by OHCQ, which is [LICENSED BED COUNT].
Moving a resident from one room or bed in the program to another, covered by ADM-06.

procedures: At licensure the manager measures each resident bedroom (wall to wall, minus closets, bathrooms and door swings) and records the functional square footage on the Room Inventory. The Room Inventory shows the room number, size, maximum occupancy (1 or 2) and the number of beds. A room under 80 square feet is not used as a single, and a room under 120 square feet is not used as a double.

The manager reconciles the Room Inventory with the license each time a resident is admitted. Before an admission, the manager counts the beds in use and confirms that the total will not exceed the licensed bed count of [LICENSED BED COUNT]. Admission is refused if it would exceed that number.

The manager confirms that each bed is a standard bed with a mattress and is not a rollaway or cot. Each room has a door that latches, window shades or coverings and closet space for the resident's belongings. Any defect is repaired before the room is assigned (DL-03).

The manager reviews the Resident Assessment Tool, and the delegating nurse's review, to identify mobility, fall risk, cognitive, behavioral, infection-control, privacy and bathroom needs that affect the room choice (ADM-03).

The manager asks the resident about preferences such as private or shared room, location, proximity to the dining room or nursing station, roommate and religious or cultural needs. The preferences are recorded on the Bed and Room Assignment Record, and the manager honors them when reasonably possible.
The manager offers a single room when the resident's needs or preferences call for one and one is available, in line with the Resident Agreement and rates (RR-04).

A double room is assigned only with the informed agreement of both residents or their representatives. The manager considers gender, sleep schedule, smoking status (SAF-08), cognitive status, behavior, infection status, and the resident's expressed preference, and records the reasons for the pairing.
A resident who is a danger to a roommate, or who would be at high risk in a shared room, is not placed in a double room. The manager discusses alternatives with the delegating nurse.

The manager checks that the number of residents does not exceed the toilet, sink and tub or shower ratios (1 toilet and sink per 4 residents; 1 tub or shower per 8 residents), and that common space is at least 35 square feet per licensed bed (COMAR 10.07.14.49–.51). The check is repeated before any increase in beds or change in the layout, and OHCQ approval is obtained when the change affects the license (GOV-02).
The manager enters the resident name, room number, bed, date of assignment and roommate on the Bed and Room Assignment Record on the day of admission and initials the entry.

For a nonemergency move within the facility (for example a change in the resident's condition, a roommate conflict or a request from the resident), the manager gives the resident and representative at least 5 calendar days' written notice of the proposed move. The manager obtains the resident's consent, explains the reason and follows ADM-06.

A move at the resident's own request needs no waiting period once the resident or representative asks in writing and the manager confirms a suitable bed. The manager records the request and the date on the Bed and Room Assignment Record.

If the resident does not consent to a nonemergency move, the move does not take place. The manager records the refusal and works with the resident, the representative and the delegating nurse on another solution, and ADM-08 applies only if the program can no longer meet the resident's needs.

The manager updates the service plan, the emergency evacuation list (SAF-06), medication cart and room labels, and notifies the resident's physician, pharmacy and other affected providers after any change.

The manager reviews the Bed and Room Assignment Record monthly against the license, and the QA committee reviews it quarterly (GOV-04). The record is kept as part of the program's administrative records and is available to OHCQ surveyors.

responsibilities.duty: Measures rooms, makes assignments, confirms the licensed bed count, obtains consent for moves and keeps the Bed and Room Assignment Record.
Advises on clinical and safety factors that affect room assignment and roommate pairing.
Report roommate conflicts and unsafe room conditions and help residents with moves.
Repair beds, doors, shades and closets so rooms meet standards.
State room and roommate preferences and give or withhold consent to a move.

documentation: Room Inventory showing functional square footage and maximum occupancy per room
Bed and Room Assignment Record (assignments and all changes)

policies.title: Resident Assessment and Reassessment (Resident Assessment Tool)
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Manager, delegating nurse, direct care staff, residents and resident representatives
policies.purpose: To assess each resident's needs and abilities before admission and at set intervals and after changes in condition, so that the service plan and the level of care remain accurate.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses the OHCQ Resident Assessment Tool (RAT) for every assessment (COMAR 10.07.14.02). The RAT is completed within the 30 days before admission and is reviewed every 6 months (COMAR 10.07.14.22). A full assessment is done within 48 hours after a significant change or a nonroutine hospitalization, and at least annually (COMAR 10.07.14.28). The delegating nurse reassesses the resident within 48 hours of readmission (COMAR 10.07.14.29). The delegating nurse reviews the manager's assessments and has clinical oversight (COMAR 10.07.14.21). Each assessment is based on observation, interview of the resident and representative, records and the nursing assessment, and is placed in the resident record.

definitions.definition: The OHCQ-approved assessment form used to assess a resident's needs and abilities.

A change in the resident's condition as defined in COMAR 10.07.14.02. The program also treats any marked decline or improvement in physical, cognitive, behavioral or functional status, as judged by the delegating nurse or manager, as a trigger for assessment.
A hospital admission, observation stay or emergency department stay that is not a planned routine procedure. When in doubt, the stay is treated as nonroutine.
The registered nurse who has signed the agreement with the program, has completed the Board of Nursing delegating nurse course, and has clinical oversight of residents (COMAR 10.07.14.21).
Any assessment after admission, whether the 6-month review, an annual full assessment or an assessment after a significant change or hospitalization.

procedures: The manager completes the RAT within the 30 days before the admission date, with input from the applicant, the representative, the physician's information and the pre-admission screening (ADM-01). The manager signs and dates it, and the delegating nurse reviews it before the admission decision.

The delegating nurse performs a nursing assessment at or soon after admission, as part of the basis for the service plan. The nursing assessment covers health conditions, medications, skin, mobility, nutrition, cognition, behaviors and special care needs.

The manager reviews the RAT every 6 months, counted from the admission date or the most recent review, and records the review date. A tickler list is kept in the manager's office so that no review passes its due date.

The delegating nurse reviews each assessment completed by the manager and signs or initials that review. The nurse may issue nursing orders to change care or may require reassessment when the findings are incomplete or inconsistent with the resident's condition.
A full assessment on the RAT is done at least once every 12 months. The manager and delegating nurse complete it together, and the resident and representative are invited to contribute.

Direct care staff report a possible significant change to the manager or delegating nurse the same shift (HLT-04). Examples include new confusion, a fall with injury, weight loss, new incontinence, a new skin problem, a decline in eating or mobility, new behaviors or a major mood change.
When a possible significant change is reported, the manager and delegating nurse decide the same day whether it is a significant change. The decision and reasons are written in the record (REC-02).

If the change is significant, or the resident returns from a nonroutine hospitalization, the manager completes a full assessment within 48 hours of the change or the return. The delegating nurse reviews it within that time.

When a resident is readmitted from a hospital or other facility, the delegating nurse reassesses the resident within 48 hours of readmission. The nurse reviews the discharge orders, medication changes, treatment orders and any new care needs, and reconciles medications with the pharmacy and prescriber (HLT-01).

After every reassessment, the manager and delegating nurse decide whether the resident's needs remain within the licensed level of care and the retention limits (ADM-05). If they do not, the manager starts the planning process in ADM-07 or ADM-08 and notifies the resident and representative.

After every reassessment, the service plan is reviewed and revised within the time set in ADM-04. The manager notifies the resident, representative and the physician of changes that affect care or services.

The manager gives the resident and representative the results of the assessment and explains them in plain language and in the resident's preferred language (RR-08). The resident's own views about needs and preferences are recorded.

The manager places each RAT, nursing assessment and review in the resident record (REC-01). Completed assessments are available to OHCQ surveyors, who may compare them with the observed condition of the resident.

The manager audits at least 10 percent of records each quarter, or every record if there are fewer than 10 residents, to check that assessments were done on time and signed by the delegating nurse. The results are reported to the QA committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Completes the RAT at the required times, tracks due dates, starts a full assessment after a significant change or nonroutine hospitalization and updates the service plan.
Performs nursing assessments, reviews the manager's assessments, reassesses within 48 hours of readmission and recommends changes in care or level.
Observe and report changes in condition at once.
Give information, take part in the assessment and receive the results.
Reviews audit results on timeliness and completeness of assessments.

policies.title: Service Plan
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Manager, delegating nurse, direct care staff, residents and resident representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure that each resident has a written, individualized service plan, based on assessed needs and preferences, that guides staff in providing care and is kept current.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] writes a service plan for each resident within 30 calendar days of admission, based on the Resident Assessment Tool and the nursing assessment (COMAR 10.07.14.28). The service plan is reviewed every 6 months. It is also revised after a full assessment following a significant change or nonroutine hospitalization, and after the annual full assessment. The plan addresses the resident's special care needs, including falls, pressure ulcers, diabetes, oxygen, enteral feeding, catheter, ostomy, mental illness and behaviors. The resident and the representative are invited to service plan meetings. The service plan is kept in the resident record (COMAR 10.07.14.29) and is followed by all staff.

definitions.definition: The written, individualized plan that states the resident's needs, the services to be provided, who provides them, how often, and the resident's goals and preferences.
Conditions that need specific attention in the plan: falls, pressure ulcers, diabetes, oxygen, enteral feeding, catheter, ostomy, mental illness and behaviors.
A meeting at which the manager, delegating nurse as needed, the resident and the representative review and agree on the plan.
The OHCQ assessment form (see ADM-03).

procedures: At admission, the manager records the date by which the service plan is due, which is 30 calendar days from the admission date, on the tickler list.

Within the first days after admission, direct care staff follow an interim care plan based on the RAT, the physician's orders and the delegating nurse's instructions, so that care is safe until the service plan is written.
The manager drafts the service plan from the RAT and the nursing assessment (ADM-03), and from the resident's own statements of needs, routines, goals and preferences (RR-06).

The plan states each need identified, the service or intervention, who delivers it (for example direct care staff, a certified medication technician or the delegating nurse), how often, and any equipment needed. It includes personal care, medication help, meals and diet, mobility, activities, social and spiritual needs, and communication needs.

The manager and delegating nurse check each of the special care needs and write specific interventions for those that apply. These are falls (HLT-06), pressure ulcers (HLT-07), diabetes, oxygen, enteral feeding, catheter, ostomy, mental illness and behaviors (HLT-05). If a need is not applicable, the plan says so.
The plan names who monitors each special care need, how, and how often, and states when the staff must notify the delegating nurse or the physician (HLT-04).

At least 7 days before the meeting, the manager invites the resident and the representative, in writing and verbally, to the service plan meeting. The manager offers a time that suits them and arranges an interpreter or auxiliary aid if needed (RR-08).

At the meeting the manager reviews the plan in plain language and asks for the resident's agreement, preferences and changes. The manager records who attended, and if the resident or representative does not attend, the manager records the invitation and the effort made to include them.

The manager revises the plan to reflect the discussion. The resident or representative is offered a copy. The manager, the delegating nurse where nursing needs are involved, and the resident or representative sign and date the plan.

Within 3 days of finalization, the manager reviews the plan with direct care staff on each shift and certified medication technicians. Staff sign the Plan Review Sheet to show that they know the plan. The care assignment sheet used by staff is updated to match.

The plan is reviewed at least every 6 months by the manager and the delegating nurse, with the resident and representative invited. The review confirms whether the services are working, and any change is written into the plan.

After a full assessment due to a significant change, a nonroutine hospitalization or the annual assessment, the manager updates the service plan promptly. The update is completed within the time needed to protect the resident and no later than the next service plan meeting. The manager then notifies the resident and representative of the changes.

If the resident refuses a service in the plan, the manager discusses the risks with the resident and representative, documents the refusal and the discussion, notifies the physician and delegating nurse, and revises the plan to reflect the resident's choice, within the limits of resident safety (RR-01).

Care staff document the services delivered according to the plan and in the care notes at least weekly and on events (COMAR 10.07.14.29; REC-02). The manager spot-checks care notes against the plan monthly.
The manager keeps all versions of the service plan in the resident record (REC-01), and reports the percentage of plans completed on time and reviewed on time to the QA committee quarterly (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Writes the plan within 30 calendar days, invites the resident and representative, ensures every special care need is addressed, and reviews it every 6 months.
Provides the nursing assessment and orders, contributes to the plan, and reviews plans for nursing needs.

responsibilities.duty: Follow the plan, document care and report changes.
Take part in the meeting, state preferences and agree to or question the plan.
