policies.title: Retention Limits and Conditions the Program Cannot Serve
policies.applies_to: All residents; Assisted Living Manager, Alternate Manager, Delegating Nurse, direct care staff
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] serves a resident only while the resident's needs can be safely met within the licensed level of care and the admission limits that Maryland sets, and to give a clear, fair process when a resident's needs exceed what the program may provide.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is licensed by the MDH Office of Health Care Quality (OHCQ) for a stated number of beds at a stated level of care: Level 1 (low), Level 2 (moderate) or Level 3 (high). Under COMAR 10.07.14.05 a resident may be served only within the licensed level. A resident may remain in the program only while the resident's needs fall within that level and within the limits of COMAR 10.07.14.23B-C. The program does not retain a resident who needs more than intermittent nursing care, treatment of a stage 3 or stage 4 pressure ulcer, ventilator services, skilled monitoring of a fluctuating acute condition, or monitoring of a chronic condition that cannot be controlled. The program also does not retain a resident who is dangerous to self or others, or at high risk, where that risk cannot be managed in the program (COMAR 10.07.14.23C). Hospice care is a limited exception under COMAR 10.07.14.23D and is handled under HLT-08. Level-of-care waivers for an individual resident are used only where OHCQ regulations allow them and only with the approvals those regulations require. The Assisted Living Manager does not rely on an informal or undocumented exception. When a resident's needs exceed what the program may serve, the Manager starts discharge planning promptly and gives at least 30 calendar days' written notice for a nonemergency discharge (COMAR 10.07.14.34), as set out in ADM-08. Retention decisions are never based on race, color, national origin, sexual orientation, gender identity, religion, or physical or mental disability (COMAR 10.07.14.23A) and are made on documented, individualized assessment of needs and risks.

definitions.definition: The level (1, 2 or 3) and bed count stated on the program's OHCQ license. Residents may be served only within this level.
Nursing services needed on a periodic, not continuous, basis. Needs beyond this are outside the admission and retention limits of COMAR 10.07.14.23B.
A change in a resident's physical, cognitive, behavioral or functional condition that is expected to last, or that alters the care the resident needs.
The registered nurse who has a signed agreement with the program and who assesses residents and oversees delegated nursing tasks. See HLT-03.
An immediate transfer to a hospital or other setting because the resident's condition or behavior poses an imminent danger to the resident or others.

procedures: The Assisted Living Manager posts the licensed level of care and bed count where staff can see them and confirms them against the OHCQ license at least annually (see GOV-02).

The Delegating Nurse reviews each resident's needs against the licensed level and the COMAR 10.07.14.23B-C limits at every reassessment, after any significant change, and within 48 hours after a nonroutine hospitalization (see ADM-03).

Any staff member who sees a change in a resident's condition, behavior or care needs reports it to the Delegating Nurse or the Manager the same shift and records it in the resident record (see HLT-04 and REC-02).

The Delegating Nurse screens each reported change against the retention limits: need for more than intermittent nursing care, stage 3 or 4 pressure ulcer treatment, ventilator services, skilled monitoring of a fluctuating acute condition, uncontrollable chronic condition, or danger/high risk that cannot be managed.

If a need could be met by adding services or interventions within the licensed level (for example, a service plan revision, home health or therapy, or increased staff supervision), the Manager and Delegating Nurse revise the service plan under ADM-04 and set a date to re-evaluate.

If the resident is receiving hospice, the Manager follows HLT-08 and applies the hospice exception only as COMAR 10.07.14.23D allows. The Manager documents the hospice agency's plan of care and the program's ability to meet the resident's needs with hospice support.

If a resident-specific level-of-care waiver is requested or considered, the Manager confirms with OHCQ in writing that the waiver is available and approved before relying on it. The approval is filed in the resident record, and the resident or representative is told of any conditions.

When the Delegating Nurse and Manager determine that needs exceed what the program may serve, the Manager documents the specific limit exceeded and the basis for the determination in the resident record.

Within 2 business days of that determination, the Manager meets with the resident and the resident representative (in person or by phone) to explain the reason, discuss options, and begin discharge planning. For a Medicaid waiver resident, the Manager also contacts the resident's case manager.

The Manager gives written notice of discharge at least 30 calendar days before the discharge date for a nonemergency discharge, stating the reason, the effective date, and the resident's right to complain (see ADM-08 and RR-02). The Manager provides ombudsman contact information (see RR-03).

The Manager, Delegating Nurse and resident/representative identify appropriate alternative settings, such as a higher level assisted living program, nursing facility or hospital-level care, and help arrange visits, transportation, records transfer and physician orders.

Care and services continue at the current level of safety and supervision until the resident leaves. If the resident's condition changes so that the risk becomes imminent, the Manager follows the emergency transfer steps in HLT-04 and ADM-07.

For an emergency discharge, staff call 911 as needed, send the emergency data sheet with the resident, notify the representative and physician immediately, and report as required under REC-03. The Manager then completes the written notice and discharge steps in ADM-08 as soon as practicable.
The Manager does not admit or readmit a person who, at the time of readmission, exceeds the limits above; readmission is evaluated through ADM-01 and the post-hospital reassessment in ADM-07.

The Manager reports retention determinations and discharges for needs-exceeded reasons to the QA Committee quarterly to identify patterns that may point to a need for admission screening changes (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Makes the final retention decision with the Delegating Nurse, obtains any OHCQ approval, gives notice, and leads discharge planning.
Assesses needs against the licensed level and admission limits, documents findings and recommends service plan changes or discharge.
Observe and report changes in condition or behavior promptly and document care notes.
Participate in planning, receive notice, and may exercise complaint and ombudsman rights.
Reviews retention and discharge trends and recommends improvements.

documentation: Reassessment and Resident Assessment Tool entries showing review against the licensed level and admission limits
Written determination by the Delegating Nurse and Manager stating the limit exceeded
Any OHCQ approval for a resident-specific level-of-care waiver
Records of meetings with the resident/representative and case manager
Copy of the written discharge notice with date delivered
Quarterly QA review summary of retention-related discharges

policies.title: Change in Resident's Accommodation Procedure
policies.applies_to: All residents; Assisted Living Manager, Delegating Nurse, direct care and housekeeping staff
policies.purpose: To make sure that any move of a resident to a different room or bed within [AGENCY NAME] is made with notice and consent, in a suitable room, with the resident's care and records kept current.
policies.policy: This policy meets OHCQ Application, Step Three, item 5(b), p. 10 — Change in Resident's Accommodation Procedure. A nonemergency relocation of a resident within the facility occurs only with at least 5 calendar days' notice to the resident (and representative) and the resident's consent, as required by COMAR 10.07.14.34. The new room must meet the requirements of COMAR 10.07.14.49–.51: no more than 2 residents per room, minimum room size (80 square feet for one resident and 120 square feet for two), and adequate toilet, sink and tub/shower access (1 toilet and sink per 4 residents and 1 tub/shower per 8). The bed assignment record is updated, the representative is notified, and the service plan is updated if the move affects care. A resident is never moved as a penalty or solely for staff convenience. An emergency move needed to protect the safety of a resident or others may occur without the 5-day notice but is documented and followed immediately by notice to the resident and representative. Room assignments are otherwise made under ADM-02.

definitions.definition: A planned move of a resident to a different room or bed in the same program that is not needed to address immediate danger.
The agreement of the resident, or the resident representative when the resident lacks capacity, documented in the record.
A move within the facility required immediately to protect health or safety, such as a fire or utility failure, or an imminent danger from another resident.
The program's current log showing each resident's room and bed.

procedures: The Assisted Living Manager identifies the reason for a proposed room change (resident request, change in care needs, roommate incompatibility, room repairs, or program need) and documents it in the resident record.

The Manager confirms the proposed new room meets the 2-per-room limit, the room-size requirements and the toilet, sink and bathing ratios of COMAR 10.07.14.49–.51, and is within the licensed level and bed count.

The Manager, with the Delegating Nurse when needed, checks whether the new room is suitable for the resident's needs (for example, mobility, falls risk, proximity to staff, dementia care needs, oxygen use) and for any roommate.
The Manager meets with the resident and the resident representative (in person or by phone) and explains the reason, the proposed room, and the proposed date.

The Manager gives written notice at least 5 calendar days before a nonemergency move, and obtains the consent of the resident or the representative. The signed consent is placed in the record. If the resident declines, the move does not proceed and the Manager documents the refusal and explores alternatives.
If the new room is shared, the Manager tells the proposed roommate (or representative) and obtains their agreement, and records that the roommates have been introduced.
For a Medicaid waiver resident, the Manager notifies the resident's case manager of the move.
On the move date, staff help the resident move belongings, check that all personal property is moved and not lost, and inventory items per RR-05 if the resident has a property list.
Housekeeping and maintenance prepare the new room (clean, working call/safety devices and furnishings), and staff confirm the resident can locate the bathroom, exits and call system.
The Manager or designee updates the bed assignment record the same day and the resident's room number on the medication administration record, emergency data sheet, evacuation list and other records.
The Delegating Nurse reviews whether the move affects care and, if so, revises the service plan under ADM-04 within the timeframe the nurse sets and records the changes.
The Manager notifies the resident representative of the completed move by the end of the day it occurs, and documents the notification.

For an emergency relocation, staff move the resident immediately to a safe, appropriate room, notify the Manager and the representative as soon as possible, and document the reason, time and notification. The Manager then provides the written notice and obtains consent for any continuing placement in the new room.
Within 7 days after the move, the Manager or Delegating Nurse follows up with the resident to check adjustment and satisfaction, and records the result. Complaints go to RR-02.

responsibilities.duty: Approves moves, ensures notice and consent, confirms room standards, and updates the bed assignment record.
Reviews care implications and updates the service plan when a move affects care.
Assist with the move, protect personal property, and monitor the resident's adjustment.
Prepare the new room and confirm the room is safe and ready.
Receive notice, consent or decline, and raise concerns.

documentation: Reason for the room change in the resident record
Written 5-day notice and signed consent (or documented refusal)
Updated bed assignment record
Representative notification note
Service plan revisions, if any
Property inventory update, if applicable
Emergency move documentation, if applicable

policies.title: Transferring a Resident to Another Facility Procedure
policies.applies_to: All residents; Assisted Living Manager, Delegating Nurse, medication technicians, direct care staff
policies.purpose: To make sure that when a resident is transferred to a hospital or another facility, the receiving provider gets the information needed for safe care, the representative and nurse are notified, and the resident is promptly reassessed on return.
policies.policy: This policy meets OHCQ Application, Step Three, item 5(c), p. 10 — Transferring of Resident to Another Facility Procedure. For an acute transfer (for example to an emergency department or hospital), staff send an emergency data sheet with the resident, as required by COMAR 10.07.14.34. For a nonacute transfer to another facility, the Manager does discharge planning with the resident and representative and prepares transfer documents. At the time of any transfer, staff notify the resident representative and the Delegating Nurse. When a resident returns, the Delegating Nurse reassesses the resident within 48 hours of readmission (COMAR 10.07.14.29), and a full assessment and service plan update follow after a nonroutine hospitalization (COMAR 10.07.14.28). Medications, personal property and records are handled so that nothing is lost in transit. Resident rights, privacy and choice of destination are respected, and information is shared only as permitted by RR-07.

definitions.definition: A one- or two-page summary sent with a resident during acute transfer, containing identifying information, diagnoses, allergies, current medications, physician and representative contacts, advance directive/code status, and baseline function.
An urgent transfer to a hospital or emergency department because of a sudden change in condition or emergency.
A planned transfer to another facility, such as another assisted living program or nursing facility.
A hospital admission other than a planned, routine one. Examples include an emergency admission or a stay following a change in condition.
The resident's return to the program after a hospital or facility stay.

procedures: The staff member who finds a resident in an emergency calls 911 when needed, stays with the resident, and notifies the Delegating Nurse and the Manager immediately (see HLT-04).

A designated staff member completes or updates the emergency data sheet, kept in each resident's record in a place all staff know, and sends a copy with the resident in the ambulance. The sheet includes code status or advance directive information (see RR-06).

Staff send a current medication list or the medication administration record copy, the resident's identification, and the representative's contact information with the resident. The Manager does not delay emergency transport to prepare additional documents.

At the time of transfer, staff notify the resident representative and the Delegating Nurse by phone, and notify the physician or prescriber as set out in HLT-04. The time and person notified are documented.

For a nonacute transfer, the Manager meets with the resident and representative and begins discharge planning, including identifying the receiving facility, confirming acceptance and the transfer date, and arranging transportation.

The Manager prepares transfer documents for the receiving facility: a transfer summary, current medication list and physician orders, the latest assessment and service plan, immunization and TB information, advance directives, and contacts. Copies are limited to what is needed and are released under RR-07.
The Delegating Nurse gives a nurse-to-nurse or staff-to-staff verbal report to the receiving facility when possible and records the person who received it.

Staff inventory the resident's belongings and medications that leave with the resident, record them, and secure remaining property and any controlled substance under HLT-01. The Manager follows RR-05 for resident funds.
If the resident is a Medicaid waiver participant, the Manager notifies the resident's case manager of the transfer.

For hospital stays, the Manager or designee contacts the hospital within 2 business days to learn the expected discharge date and any new care needs, and asks about the resident's wishes about returning.

Before readmission, the Manager and Delegating Nurse obtain the discharge orders and summary and determine whether the program may still serve the resident under ADM-05. If it cannot, the Manager follows ADM-08.
On the day of readmission, staff review new orders with the prescriber or Delegating Nurse, reconcile medications, and update the medication administration record per HLT-01 and HLT-02.

The Delegating Nurse reassesses the resident within 48 hours of readmission and documents the assessment in the record. After a nonroutine hospitalization, a full assessment using the Resident Assessment Tool is completed within 48 hours and the service plan is updated under ADM-04.
The Manager notifies the representative of the return, new orders and the revised service plan. The incident is reported under SAF-02 and REC-03 if required.
The Manager records each transfer and return in the resident record (date, time, reason, destination, notifications, items sent) and reports transfer patterns to the QA Committee quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Directs the transfer process, completes discharge planning for nonacute transfers, and ensures notifications and documentation.
Gives clinical report, reviews orders, and completes the reassessment within 48 hours of readmission.
Call for help, send the emergency data sheet and medications list, and document care and notifications.
Is notified at the time of transfer and takes part in planning.

documentation: Emergency data sheet (copy kept in record)
Transfer summary and documents sent
Notification log: representative, Delegating Nurse, physician, case manager
Property and medication inventory at transfer and return
Readmission reassessment within 48 hours and updated service plan
Incident report, if applicable

policies.title: Resident Discharge, Relocation and Notice Procedure
policies.applies_to: All residents; Assisted Living Manager, Delegating Nurse, business office, direct care staff
policies.purpose: To make sure that a resident who is discharged from [AGENCY NAME] receives proper written notice, a safe and planned move, an accurate final accounting, and return of all funds and property.
policies.policy: This policy meets OHCQ Application, Step Three, item 5(d), p. 10 — Resident Discharge Procedure. [AGENCY NAME] gives at least 30 calendar days' written notice before a nonemergency discharge, as required by COMAR 10.07.14.34. The program plans the discharge with the resident and representative and, for a Medicaid waiver resident, coordinates with the case manager. Case manager visits and cooperation are a condition of waiver participation (COMAR 10.09.54.05). Transfer documents are prepared for the receiving provider. Within 30 calendar days of discharge, the program issues a final statement, pays any refund due, and returns the resident's property and funds. The resident record is kept for 5 years after discharge (COMAR 10.07.14.29). Discharge is permitted only for a reason in the resident agreement and these policies, such as needs exceeding the licensed level (ADM-05), nonpayment after due process, or program closure, and never in retaliation for a complaint or use of resident rights. An emergency discharge is handled as ADM-05 and ADM-07 provide.

definitions.definition: A discharge initiated by the program that is not needed to address immediate danger, and which requires 30 calendar days' written notice.
The process of identifying the resident's post-discharge needs and a safe destination, and arranging services, transportation, medications and records.
A written accounting of all charges, payments, deposits and refunds due at discharge.
For a Medicaid Community Options Waiver resident, the person who coordinates the resident's waiver services and visits at least quarterly.

procedures: The Assisted Living Manager documents the reason for a proposed discharge and confirms it is a permitted reason under the resident agreement and ADM-05, with the Delegating Nurse's assessment where the reason is clinical.
The Manager meets with the resident and the representative to discuss the reason and begin discharge planning. For a waiver resident, the Manager contacts the case manager the same day.

The Manager delivers written notice at least 30 calendar days before the discharge date for a nonemergency discharge. The notice states the reason, the date, the resident's right to file a complaint or appeal, and ombudsman contact information (see RR-02 and RR-03). Delivery is documented by the date and the person who received it.
The Manager sends or gives a copy of the notice to the representative and records it in the resident record.

The Manager and Delegating Nurse help the resident identify and choose a destination, offering at least [NUMBER] suitable options where available, and help arrange visits, applications, transportation and any needed services such as home health.

The Delegating Nurse prepares a discharge summary and transfer documents: current medications and orders, latest assessment and service plan, treatments, diet, allergies, immunizations, advance directives and contacts. Disclosure is limited to what is needed (see RR-07).

The Delegating Nurse reviews medications with the resident or receiving provider, and staff release medications under HLT-01. Controlled substances are released or destroyed only as that policy allows and documented.
Staff meet with the resident and representative a second time before discharge to review the plan, transportation, medication supply, follow-up appointments and contacts.
On the day of discharge, staff inventory personal property with the resident or representative and obtain a signed receipt for property and medications released.
The business office prepares a final statement showing charges through the discharge date, deposits and any refund due, following the agreement terms (see RR-04).

The Manager returns the final statement, any refund and the resident's funds and property within 30 calendar days of discharge, and records the date and method. Resident funds are accounted for under RR-05.

If the discharge is an emergency, the Manager follows ADM-05 and ADM-07 and then issues written notice and the final statement as soon as practicable, and always within the 30-day period for refunds and property.

If the resident or representative objects, the Manager reviews the objection with the resident, offers the complaint process in RR-02, and does not carry out a nonemergency discharge on shorter notice.

The Manager reports the discharge as required (see REC-03) and updates the bed assignment record, resident roster, and billing, including notice to Medicaid or other payers where applicable (see GOV-06).
The Manager closes the record and retains it for 5 years after discharge, stored securely and disposed of as required by Health-General Title 4, Subtitle 3 (see REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Issues notice, leads discharge planning, ensures final statement, refunds and property are returned within 30 days.
Prepares the clinical transfer information and medication reconciliation.
Prepares the final statement and processes refunds.
Coordinates waiver services and the transition for waiver residents.
Participate in planning, receive notice, and may use complaint and ombudsman rights.

documentation: Documented reason for discharge and supporting assessment
30-day written notice with proof of delivery
Discharge planning meeting notes and case manager contacts
Discharge summary and transfer documents
Property and medication release receipts
Final statement and refund record (date and method)
Closed record retained 5 years after discharge

policies.title: Resident's Request to Terminate an Agreement Procedure
policies.applies_to: All residents and resident representatives; Assisted Living Manager, Delegating Nurse, business office
policies.purpose: To give residents and representatives a clear, respectful way to end their resident agreement and leave [AGENCY NAME], with the notice period, refund terms and final accounting stated in advance.
policies.policy: This policy meets OHCQ Application, Step Three, item 5(e), p. 10 — Resident's Request to Terminate an Agreement Procedure. A resident or the resident representative may ask to end the resident agreement at any time. [AGENCY NAME] accepts a written request. The notice period and refund terms are those stated in the resident agreement, whose financial terms are required by COMAR 10.07.14.27: the resident gives [NOTICE PERIOD IN DAYS AS STATED IN THE RESIDENT AGREEMENT] days' written notice, and the agency refunds prepaid charges and deposits as the agreement provides (see RR-04). The program holds a discharge-planning meeting and notifies the representative. The final statement, refunds and return of property are completed within 30 calendar days (COMAR 10.07.14.34). The program does not discourage, delay or penalize a resident for asking to terminate, and continues to give care and services until the resident leaves.

definitions.definition: The written contract between the resident and [AGENCY NAME], including the financial terms, notice and refund provisions.
A written request by the resident or representative to end the resident agreement and leave the program.
A person legally authorized or designated by the resident to act for the resident (see RR-01).
The written accounting of charges, payments, deposits and refunds at the end of the agreement.

procedures: Any staff member who receives a verbal request to terminate the agreement tells the Assisted Living Manager the same day and helps the resident put it in writing if the resident wishes. A verbal request is also recorded in the resident record.
The Manager accepts the written request from the resident or representative, dates it on receipt, and gives the resident a copy marked as received.

The Manager checks the resident's authority: if a representative makes the request, the Manager confirms the representative's authority and, wherever the resident can express a wish, confirms the resident's wishes.

Within 2 business days of receipt, the Manager meets with the resident and representative to confirm the requested move-out date, review the notice period and refund terms in the resident agreement, and ask whether any concerns could be resolved. The Manager does not pressure the resident to stay. Any complaint is recorded and handled under RR-02.

The Manager states in writing the effective termination date, the notice period under the agreement, and the amount of any charges for the notice period, and gives it to the resident and representative.

The Manager holds a discharge-planning meeting with the resident, representative and the Delegating Nurse covering the destination, transportation, services needed after the move, medication supply and follow-up care.
For a Medicaid waiver resident, the Manager notifies the case manager of the request and coordinates the transition and any waiver service changes.
The Manager notifies the representative of the plan and date, and documents notifications.
The Delegating Nurse prepares the discharge summary, medication list and transfer documents, and staff release medications under HLT-01 and ADM-08.
Care and services continue under the current service plan until the resident leaves.
On the move-out date, staff inventory and return personal property and obtain a signed receipt.
The business office prepares the final statement showing charges through the termination date, deposits, prepaid amounts and refunds, applying the terms in the resident agreement.

The Manager provides the final statement, any refund and funds held for the resident, and all property within 30 calendar days of the resident's departure, and records the date and method (see RR-05).

If the resident leaves without the notice period or in an emergency, the Manager still issues the final statement and returns refunds and property within 30 calendar days, applying only the charges the agreement permits.
The Manager updates the bed assignment record and roster, reports as required under REC-03, and retains the closed record for 5 years after discharge (see REC-01).
The Manager reviews termination requests and their stated reasons with the QA Committee quarterly to find areas for improvement (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Accepts the request, explains notice and refund terms, leads planning and ensures the final accounting within 30 days.
Prepares clinical transfer information and medication reconciliation.
Prepares the final statement and issues refunds.
Report requests to the Manager and continue care until departure.
Submit the request in writing and take part in discharge planning.

documentation: Written termination request with date received
Manager's written confirmation of termination date and notice period
Discharge-planning meeting notes and representative notifications
Case manager contact for waiver residents
Property and medication release receipts
Final statement and refund record
Closed record retained 5 years after discharge

policies.title: Medication Management, Storage and Disposal
policies.applies_to: All residents; Assisted Living Manager, Delegating Nurse, certified medication technicians, direct care staff, consultant pharmacist
policies.purpose: To make sure that medications are managed, stored, administered, documented and disposed of safely and in compliance with COMAR 10.07.14.31 and the Board of Nursing delegation rules in COMAR 10.27.11.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] manages resident medications in accordance with COMAR 10.07.14.31. Unlicensed staff who administer medications must have completed the Maryland Board of Nursing medication technician course and be certified, and must administer under delegation that complies with COMAR 10.27.11 (see HLT-02). A medication regimen review is completed within 14 calendar days of admission. Each resident's ability to self-administer is assessed, and the Delegating Nurse reassesses self-administration quarterly. A pharmacist conducts an on-site review at least every 6 months for any resident taking 9 or more medications; findings are documented and reviewed in QA (see GOV-04). The Delegating Nurse reviews medication administration on site at least every 45 calendar days. Medications are stored securely and documented as COMAR 10.07.14.31 requires. Controlled substances are counted every shift, kept under double lock, and destroyed on site and documented. Medications are given only on a current prescriber's order.

definitions.definition: An unlicensed staff member who completed the Board of Nursing medication technician course and is certified to administer medications under delegation.
The registered nurse who delegates medication administration, assesses residents and oversees staff under COMAR 10.27.11.
A review of each resident's medications for appropriateness, interactions, duplications, side effects and allergies, completed within 14 calendar days of admission.
A resident's taking of his or her own medications after a nurse assessment finds the resident able to do so safely.
A medication in a federal or state controlled drug schedule, such as an opioid or benzodiazepine.
The record in which each dose given, refused, held or missed is documented.

procedures: The Assisted Living Manager keeps a list of staff who may administer medications, with each person's Board of Nursing certification and its expiration, and confirms no uncertified person administers medications (see HLT-02).
At admission, the Delegating Nurse obtains written or verified prescriber orders for every medication, treatment and supplement, including over-the-counter products, and the resident's allergies.
The Delegating Nurse completes the medication regimen review within 14 calendar days of admission, documents any questions to the prescriber, and records the outcome.

The Delegating Nurse assesses whether the resident can self-administer safely and records the assessment. If self-administration is approved, medications are stored as the assessment directs, and the Delegating Nurse reassesses the resident quarterly or sooner after any change in condition. If the resident can no longer do so safely, staff administer and the service plan is updated.

Each medication is received from the pharmacy or family in a labeled container, checked against the order by a nurse or CMT, logged in the medication receiving record, and placed in secure storage the same shift.

Medications are stored in a locked cabinet or room or locked cart, separated by resident, with external-use products separate from internal-use products and refrigerated medications in a locked refrigerator or locked box with a thermometer. Access is limited to authorized staff and keys are controlled.

Staff check storage areas and refrigerator temperature at least daily and record the results. Staff remove expired, discontinued or recalled medications from the supply and follow the disposal steps in this policy.

Authorized staff administer medications at the ordered time using the MAR, check the resident's identity, give the right dose and route, and document each dose immediately after giving it. Refusals, held doses and errors are documented and reported to the Delegating Nurse the same shift.
Staff report any medication error or adverse reaction to the prescriber and Delegating Nurse immediately and complete an incident report under SAF-02. The Manager reviews errors for QA.

Controlled substances are kept under double lock. Two staff members count them at every shift change, record the count in the controlled substance log and sign. Any discrepancy is reported at once to the Delegating Nurse and Manager, who investigate and report as required (see SAF-01 and REC-03).

The Delegating Nurse visits the program on site and reviews medication administration at least every 45 calendar days, including observation of each resident as required, MAR accuracy, storage, controlled substance counts and staff competence, and writes findings in the record.

The consultant pharmacist reviews on site at least every 6 months for any resident on 9 or more medications. The pharmacist's written findings go to the Delegating Nurse and Manager, who contact prescribers as needed and document responses. Summaries are presented to the QA Committee.

The Manager and Delegating Nurse check that residents on psychotropic or other high-risk medications have a documented reason and monitoring, and that restrictive use of medication is not used as a restraint (see SAF-04).

When a medication is discontinued, the resident dies or leaves the program, or a medication expires, two staff members document and secure it. Noncontrolled medications are disposed of as the Delegating Nurse directs under the program's disposal procedure, and records note the drug, quantity, date and both signatures. Returned medications go to the resident or representative as ADM-08 provides, and the receipt is signed.

Controlled substances to be discarded are destroyed on site by the Delegating Nurse or Manager with a second witness, in a way that makes them unusable, and recorded in the controlled substance log with the date, drug, strength, quantity and signatures.
The Manager reviews medication records, storage, discrepancies, errors and pharmacist findings at least quarterly with the QA Committee and implements corrective actions (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures only certified, delegated staff administer medications, resources and keys are controlled, and QA reviews are completed.
Completes regimen review within 14 days, self-administration assessments with quarterly reassessment, 45-day on-site reviews, and delegation oversight.
Administer medications as ordered, document on the MAR, count controlled substances each shift, and report errors.
Reviews on site every 6 months for residents on 9 or more medications and documents findings.
Provide orders and respond to review findings.

documentation: Current prescriber orders and allergy list
Medication regimen review within 14 days of admission
Self-administration assessments and quarterly reassessments
MAR and refusal or error records
Controlled substance count log (each shift) and destruction log
Storage temperature and refrigerator logs
Delegating Nurse 45-day on-site review reports
Pharmacist 6-month review reports and responses
Disposal and return receipts
QA review minutes

policies.title: Medication Administration and Staff Authorization (Certified Medication Technicians)
policies.applies_to: All staff who administer, assist with or supervise medications, the Assisted Living Manager, the delegating nurse and the Administrator.
policies.purpose: To make sure residents receive medications safely, exactly as ordered, and only from staff who are legally authorized to give them, as required by COMAR 10.07.14.31, COMAR 10.27.11 and COMAR 10.39.04.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] allows only the following people to administer medications to residents: (1) a licensed nurse, or (2) a certified medication technician (CMT) who has completed the Maryland Board of Nursing 20-hour medication technician course, holds current Board of Nursing certification, and works under delegation from the delegating nurse. No other staff member may administer medications. Residents who are assessed as able to self-administer may do so under the self-administration assessment and delegating nurse reassessment described below. CMTs renew certification every 2 years with 100 practice hours and a 4-hour update. Proof of course completion, certification and renewal is kept in each CMT's personnel file. The delegating nurse reviews medication administration on site at least every 45 calendar days. This policy follows COMAR 10.07.14.31 and the Board of Nursing delegation rules in COMAR 10.27.11 and COMAR 10.39.04. It works with HLT-01 (storage and disposal) and HLT-03 (delegating nurse duties).

definitions.definition: An unlicensed staff member who has completed the Board of Nursing medication technician course and holds current Board of Nursing certification, as the term is used in COMAR 10.07.14.02.

The process by which the delegating nurse, a registered nurse, assigns a nursing task such as medication administration to a competent unlicensed staff member and supervises that task, as defined in COMAR 10.07.14.02 and governed by COMAR 10.27.11.
The State-required assessment instrument used to identify a resident's needs, including medication needs, as defined in COMAR 10.07.14.02.
Any dose given or omitted that differs from the practitioner's order, including wrong resident, drug, dose, route or time, and omitted or unrecorded doses.
An event as defined in COMAR 10.07.14.02 that must be reported under SAF-02. A medication error is an incident.

procedures: Authorization: The Administrator or Assisted Living Manager (ALM) assigns medication duties only to a licensed nurse or a CMT whose Board of Nursing certification has been verified. No other employee, volunteer or relief worker may administer medications.

Verification before assignment: Before a new CMT works a medication shift, the ALM verifies certification on the Board of Nursing's public lookup and prints the result. The ALM places the printout and a copy of the certificate and 20-hour course completion in the personnel file (STF-05).

Delegation: The delegating nurse completes the written delegation and competency check required by COMAR 10.27.11 before the CMT works alone. The nurse observes the CMT administer medications to residents and documents the observation. A copy goes in the personnel file.

Renewal tracking: The ALM keeps a CMT tracking log with each person's expiration date, practice hours and 4-hour update status. Renewal is every 2 years with 100 practice hours and the 4-hour update. The ALM reviews the log monthly and meets with any CMT whose expiration is within 90 days.

Lapse: If certification lapses or is not verified, the ALM removes the CMT from all medication duties the same day and notifies the delegating nurse. The CMT may return to medication duties only after the ALM verifies renewed certification.

Self-administration assessment: At admission, the delegating nurse assesses whether the resident can safely self-administer, and records the result in the resident record. The nurse reassesses at least quarterly and whenever the resident's condition changes. Residents who self-administer have locked storage in their rooms and an agreed monitoring plan in the service plan (ADM-04).

Regimen review: The delegating nurse reviews each new resident's medication regimen within 14 calendar days of admission and documents the review. The nurse reports any concerns to the prescribing practitioner.

Before each pass: The CMT washes hands and checks the order, pharmacy label and medication administration record (MAR) for the correct resident, drug, dose, route, time and any special instructions (food, vital signs, hold parameters). The CMT confirms the resident's identity.
Documenting: The CMT initials the MAR immediately after giving each dose. The CMT never pre-charts. Refusals, held doses, omitted doses and reasons are documented on the MAR and in the care notes.

PRN medications: A CMT gives a PRN medication only under a practitioner's written order with the reason, dose, frequency and maximum amount. If the resident's need does not fit the order, the CMT calls the delegating nurse for direction before giving it. The CMT documents the reason and the result.

Orders: The CMT accepts only written or properly transcribed orders. Verbal or telephone orders are taken and transcribed only by the licensed nurse. The CMT does not change, crush, split or substitute any medication unless the order or pharmacist allows it.

Medication errors: The CMT who discovers an error immediately checks on the resident, notifies the delegating nurse and, as the nurse directs, the practitioner. The CMT notifies the resident representative and completes an incident report within 24 hours of knowledge (SAF-02). The ALM reviews each error within 3 business days for cause and corrective action.

Controlled substances: Two staff count controlled substances at every shift change and sign the count record. Controlled substances are stored under double lock. Discrepancies are reported to the ALM at once. Destruction is done on site with two witnesses and documented as required by HLT-01.

Delegating nurse on-site review: At least every 45 calendar days, the delegating nurse reviews MARs, medication storage and CMT practice on site. The nurse documents findings and corrective actions in a signed visit note and gives a copy to the ALM.

Pharmacist review: For each resident taking 9 or more medications, a pharmacist performs an on-site review at least every 6 months. The ALM gives the report to the delegating nurse and prescribers. The report is also reviewed in the Quality Assurance process (GOV-04).

Retraining: The delegating nurse retrains any CMT who makes an error or fails an observation. The ALM documents the retraining. Repeated errors lead to removal from medication duties and discipline under STF-06.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure only authorized staff administer medications and that adequate resources exist for a compliant medication system.
Verifies and tracks CMT certification, assigns medication duties, reviews errors and keeps personnel file proof.
Delegates and supervises medication administration, assesses self-administration quarterly, performs the 14-day regimen review and the 45-day on-site review, and trains CMTs.
Administers medications only as ordered, documents each dose, reports errors and refusals immediately and keeps certification current.
Performs the on-site review every 6 months for residents on 9 or more medications.

documentation: CMT personnel file: Board of Nursing certificate, 20-hour course completion, renewal evidence (100 practice hours and 4-hour update), license verification printouts and delegation and competency records
CMT tracking log
Medication administration records
Self-administration assessments and quarterly reassessments
Regimen review documentation (14 days)
Controlled substance count and destruction records
Delegating nurse 45-day visit notes
Pharmacist review reports
Incident reports for medication errors

policies.title: Nursing Services and Delegating Nurse Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: The delegating nurse, alternate delegating nurse, Assisted Living Manager, Administrator and all direct care staff.
policies.purpose: To define how registered nurse oversight is provided in the assisted living program, as required by COMAR 10.07.14.21, 10.07.14.14, 10.07.14.13 and the Board of Nursing delegation rules in COMAR 10.27.11.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses a registered nurse (RN) as its delegating nurse. The delegating nurse has a signed agreement with [AGENCY NAME] and has completed the Board of Nursing delegating nurse course. The delegating nurse has clinical oversight of resident care, issues nursing orders, reviews the manager's assessments, and delegates nursing tasks to unlicensed staff in accordance with COMAR 10.27.11. The RN observes each resident on site at least every 45 days. The RN, or a qualified alternate, is on call at all times. [AGENCY NAME] provides on-site nursing services beyond these visits only when the delegating nurse or a practitioner orders them. The Assisted Living Manager (ALM) and the delegating nurse meet at least every 6 months as part of the Quality Assurance plan (COMAR 10.07.14.13 §A(2)(b)). Nursing coverage is part of the staffing plan (STF-01).

definitions.definition: The registered nurse who has signed an agreement with the program and completed the Board of Nursing delegating nurse course, and who delegates and supervises nursing tasks under COMAR 10.07.14.21.
Assignment of a nursing task to a competent unlicensed staff member under COMAR 10.07.14.02 and COMAR 10.27.11.
A direction to staff written by the delegating nurse about a resident's care or monitoring.
A second qualified RN who covers on-call duties when the primary delegating nurse is not available.
The State-required assessment instrument defined in COMAR 10.07.14.02.

procedures: Engagement: Before the program accepts residents, the Administrator signs a written agreement with the delegating nurse, [DELEGATING NURSE NAME]. The agreement states the RN's duties under COMAR 10.07.14.21, the on-call arrangement and the visit schedule.

Credentials: The Administrator verifies the RN's active Maryland license and the Board of Nursing delegating nurse course certificate. Copies go in the RN's personnel or contractor file. The Administrator re-verifies the license at each renewal.

Alternate: The Administrator names an alternate delegating nurse with the same qualifications, in writing. The on-call schedule showing who is covering is posted at the staff station and given to all shifts.

On-call access: The delegating nurse or alternate is reachable by phone at [PHONE] 24 hours a day. Staff call when a resident has a change of condition, a medication error or any situation outside the service plan. The call and the nurse's instructions are documented in the care notes.

45-day visits: The RN observes each resident in person on site at least every 45 days. The RN documents each observation in the resident record. The ALM tracks the next-due date for every resident on a visit log and reports any overdue visit to the Administrator immediately.

Assessment review: The RN reviews the ALM's Resident Assessment Tool at admission, annually, and after a significant change or nonroutine hospitalization. The RN signs the review. The RN contributes nursing assessment to the service plan (ADM-03 and ADM-04).

Nursing orders: The RN writes nursing orders in the resident record with date and signature. The ALM puts orders into the care plan and communicates them to staff at shift report. Staff follow orders as written and ask the RN when unsure.

Delegation: The RN decides which nursing tasks may be delegated, to whom and for which residents, following COMAR 10.27.11. The RN teaches the task, checks competency by observation and documents it. The RN may withdraw delegation at any time.

Training: The RN trains staff in resident-specific care needs and personal-care competency, and delegates only to staff whose competency has been checked. Competency is documented in personnel files (STF-03).

Medication oversight: The RN carries out the duties assigned in HLT-02, including quarterly self-administration reassessment, the regimen review, and the review of medication administration at least every 45 calendar days.
Change of condition: When called, the RN decides whether the resident needs practitioner contact, transfer, a nursing visit or a reassessment (HLT-04). The RN documents the decision.

Ordered on-site nursing: The program provides on-site nursing services beyond the 45-day visit only when ordered by the delegating nurse or a practitioner. The ALM schedules the nurse for the ordered time and frequency and records the order and visits.
Retention check: If a resident's needs may exceed what the program can serve, the RN advises the ALM and Administrator in writing, and the team follows ADM-05.

6-month meeting: At least every 6 months, the ALM and RN meet to review resident care, fall and skin trends, medication errors, staff competency and QA findings. Minutes are signed by both and kept with the QA plan (GOV-04).
Annual evaluation: The Administrator reviews the RN's performance and coverage annually against the agreement and COMAR 10.07.14.21, and keeps the evaluation on file.

responsibilities.duty: Signs and maintains the RN agreement, secures alternate coverage and makes sure RN visits and on-call coverage happen.
Provides clinical oversight, completes 45-day resident observations, issues nursing orders, reviews assessments, delegates and supervises tasks and remains on call.
Covers on-call and delegation duties when the primary RN is unavailable.
Completes assessments, tracks visit due dates, carries out nursing orders, calls the RN promptly and meets with the RN every 6 months.
Follow nursing orders and delegated instructions and report changes to the ALM and RN.

documentation: Signed delegating nurse agreement
RN license verification and Board of Nursing delegating nurse course certificate
Alternate RN agreement and on-call schedule
45-day visit log and resident observation notes
Signed RN reviews of assessments
Nursing orders
Delegation and competency records
Records of ordered on-site nursing
6-month ALM and RN meeting minutes
Annual RN performance evaluation

policies.title: Change of Condition, Physician Notification and Hospital Transfer
policies.applies_to: All direct care staff, Certified Medication Technicians, the Assisted Living Manager, the delegating nurse and the Administrator.
policies.purpose: To make sure every change in a resident's condition is recognized, reported, assessed and documented quickly, and that residents transferred to a hospital go with the information needed for their care, as required by COMAR 10.07.14.28, 10.07.14.29, 10.07.14.33 and 10.07.14.34.
policies.policy: Staff report any change in a resident's physical, mental or functional condition to the Assisted Living Manager (ALM) and the delegating nurse right away. [AGENCY NAME] notifies the practitioner and the resident's representative as directed by the delegating nurse. A significant change, or a nonroutine hospitalization, requires a full reassessment within 48 hours. For emergency transfers, staff call 911 first and send the emergency data sheet with the resident. When a resident returns from the hospital, the delegating nurse reassesses within 48 hours of readmission. If the change results from an incident, staff complete an incident report within 24 hours of knowledge. Staff chart care notes at least weekly and on events.

definitions.definition: A change in a resident's condition or needs as defined in COMAR 10.07.14.02 that triggers a full reassessment.
An unplanned hospital admission or emergency transfer, as distinguished from a planned, scheduled procedure.

A one-page summary that goes with a resident transferred to acute care. It includes the information required by COMAR 10.07.14.34 and the resident's identification, diagnoses, medications, allergies, practitioner, advance directives and representative contact.
An event defined in COMAR 10.07.14.02 and reportable under COMAR 10.07.14.33.
The State-required assessment instrument defined in COMAR 10.07.14.02.

procedures: Recognize: Staff watch for changes such as new confusion, fever, falls, pain, loss of appetite or fluids, new swelling or skin changes, breathing difficulty, behavior change or loss of function. Any staff member who notices a change tells the shift lead and the ALM immediately.

Check: The staff member checks the resident, takes vital signs if trained to do so, and stays with the resident. In an emergency such as chest pain, difficulty breathing, unresponsiveness, stroke signs, serious injury or choking, staff call 911 first, then the delegating nurse.

Call the delegating nurse: For all non-emergency changes, the ALM or shift lead calls the delegating nurse at [PHONE] and reports what was observed. The nurse decides on a practitioner call, a nursing visit, monitoring or transfer. The call and instructions are recorded in the care notes.

Notify the practitioner: As directed by the nurse, or immediately if the nurse cannot be reached and the change is significant, the ALM contacts the resident's practitioner and records the time, the person spoken to and any new orders. Orders are transcribed by a licensed nurse (HLT-02).

Notify the representative: The ALM notifies the resident representative and any person the resident has named by phone as soon as possible after the change or transfer. The ALM records who was told, when, and what was said. If no one can be reached, the ALM documents each attempt.
Respect preferences: Staff check the resident's advance directives and preferences before acting (RR-06) and send copies with the resident when transferred.

Emergency transfer: When 911 is called, a staff member prepares the emergency data sheet and takes it, together with the current medication list, face sheet, advance directives, representative contact information and insurance cards, to the paramedics. Staff send a copy with the resident and keep a copy in the record.

Accompany: When possible, a staff member or the representative goes with the resident or follows to the hospital. The ALM phones the hospital the same shift to give information and ask about the resident's status.

Incident report: When the change results from an incident, such as a fall, injury or medication error, the staff member who knows of it completes an incident report within 24 hours of knowledge and gives it to the ALM (SAF-02). The ALM reviews it and tells the delegating nurse. Death or injury requiring OHCQ notice is handled under SAF-02 and REC-03.

Bed hold and belongings: The ALM sends the resident's essential medications, clothing and personal items as needed and lists them. The ALM follows the bed-hold terms in the resident agreement (RR-04).

Full reassessment: Within 48 hours of any significant change or nonroutine hospitalization, the ALM completes a full reassessment using the Resident Assessment Tool, and the delegating nurse reviews and signs it (ADM-03).

Update the service plan: The ALM revises the service plan to reflect the new needs and invites the resident and representative to a meeting (ADM-04). The ALM tells staff of the changes at shift report.

Readmission: On return from the hospital, the ALM obtains discharge orders and the medication list. The delegating nurse reassesses the resident within 48 hours of readmission. The ALM reconciles medications with the practitioner and pharmacy before the next dose (HLT-01).
Retention check: If the resident's needs now exceed what the program may serve, the ALM and delegating nurse follow ADM-05 and, if needed, ADM-07 and ADM-08.

Charting: Staff write a care note for the event covering what was observed, who was notified and when, actions taken, and the resident's response. Staff also write care notes at least weekly for every resident even when there is no change (REC-02).

responsibilities.duty: Recognize and report changes immediately, call 911 in an emergency, and chart care notes.
Coordinates the response, notifies the nurse, practitioner and representative, completes reassessments within 48 hours and updates the service plan.
Directs the response, reviews assessments, reassesses within 48 hours of readmission and orders monitoring or nursing visits.
Reviews incident reports and transfers and makes sure required reports are made to the State.

documentation: Care notes with each notification (time, person, response)
Emergency data sheet copy
Incident report when applicable
Practitioner orders
Reassessment using the Resident Assessment Tool within 48 hours
Delegating nurse readmission reassessment
Updated service plan and meeting invitations
Hospital discharge paperwork
List of belongings and medications sent

policies.title: Dementia, Cognitive Impairment and Alzheimer's Special Care Unit
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Assisted Living Manager, the delegating nurse and the Administrator, and any unit that serves residents with Alzheimer's disease or related dementia.
policies.purpose: To make sure residents with dementia or cognitive impairment receive safe, person-centered care from trained staff, and that [AGENCY NAME] operates an Alzheimer's special care unit only with OHCQ's written approval, as required by COMAR 10.07.14.32, 10.07.14.19 and 10.07.14.14.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides care to residents with dementia in accordance with each resident's service plan, which addresses behaviors and other special care needs. [AGENCY NAME] will not operate or advertise an Alzheimer's special care unit until it has submitted the Alzheimer's Special Care Unit Disclosure Form to OHCQ and received OHCQ's written approval. Awake overnight staff are mandatory on an Alzheimer's special care unit under COMAR 10.07.14.32, and there is no electronic-monitoring waiver of that requirement. Personal-care staff complete 6 hours of cognitive impairment, mental illness and behavioral health training within 120 days of hire; other staff complete 2 hours. All staff then complete annual refresher training as required by COMAR 10.07.14.19. Staffing is set by the written staffing plan under COMAR 10.07.14.14 (see STF-01).

definitions.definition: A designated unit or program that is marketed or operated as providing specialized care for residents with Alzheimer's disease or related dementia and that must be approved by OHCQ under COMAR 10.07.14.32.

definitions.term: Alzheimer's Special Care Unit Disclosure Form
definitions.definition: The form submitted to OHCQ describing the unit's philosophy, admission, care, staffing, training and environment, required before approval.
Staff who are awake and on duty on site throughout the overnight hours and not asleep.

definitions.term: Cognitive impairment, mental illness and behavioral health training
definitions.definition: The training topic required for staff by COMAR 10.07.14.19.
The State-required assessment instrument defined in COMAR 10.07.14.02.

procedures: Before opening a unit: The Administrator completes the Alzheimer's Special Care Unit Disclosure Form with the program description, staffing and training, and submits it to OHCQ. The Administrator keeps the submission proof.

Wait for approval: [AGENCY NAME] does not admit residents to a unit, or describe any part of the program as a dementia or Alzheimer's unit in marketing or the Uniform Disclosure Statement, until OHCQ's written approval is received. The Administrator files the approval in the licensing file (GOV-02).

Admission screening: The Assisted Living Manager (ALM) screens each prospective resident with dementia using ADM-01. The ALM uses the Resident Assessment Tool and the delegating nurse's assessment to decide whether the program can safely serve the person and whether unit placement is appropriate (ADM-02).

Service plan: Within 30 calendar days of admission, the service plan addresses cognition, communication, wandering and elopement risk, behaviors, sleep, nutrition, toileting, falls and activities. It states staff approaches that work for the individual resident and includes personal history and preferences (ADM-04).

Behaviors: Staff try person-centered, non-drug approaches first: reducing noise, redirection, meeting unmet needs, walks and meaningful activity. Staff record the behavior, trigger, intervention and result in care notes. Staff report new or worsening behaviors to the ALM and delegating nurse, who review the service plan.
No improper restraint: Staff never use restraints for convenience or discipline, and never give or request medication to control behavior outside a practitioner's order. SAF-04 governs any restraint.
Wandering and elopement: The ALM assesses elopement risk at admission and after any change. Staff follow SAF-03, including current photographs and the missing-resident search procedure.

Overnight staffing: On any approved Alzheimer's unit, at least one staff member is awake and on duty on site every night. The schedule shows the awake overnight person. Awake overnight staffing is never replaced by cameras, door alarms or other electronic monitoring.

Staffing level: The ALM and Administrator set unit staffing in the written staffing plan. They review it whenever the Resident Assessment Tool, acuity or census changes (STF-01). Dated schedules are kept on site for 18 months.

Training within 120 days: Personal-care staff complete 6 hours of cognitive impairment, mental illness and behavioral health training within 120 days of hire. Other staff complete 2 hours. The ALM schedules training in orientation (STF-03) and records the dates, topics and trainers.

Annual training: The ALM schedules refresher training every year at the length COMAR 10.07.14.19 requires for the staff member's role: 2 hours, or 1 hour where the shorter refresher applies. The ALM tracks completion in a training log.
Proof of training: Certificates or sign-in sheets for all dementia training are kept in each personnel file (STF-05). The ALM checks files at least quarterly.

Family and representative: The ALM invites the resident representative to all service plan meetings and tells them about the unit, its costs, and any change in the resident's condition (RR-04, HLT-04).

Environment and activities: The ALM keeps the unit free of hazards, and the activities coordinator provides structured daily activities suited to cognitive ability (DL-02). Residents may have access to a safe outdoor area under supervision.

Quality review: The delegating nurse and ALM review behavior incidents, elopement events, falls and staffing for the unit at least every 6 months and report to the QA plan (GOV-04). The Administrator updates the Disclosure Form with OHCQ if the unit's program changes.

responsibilities.duty: Submits the Disclosure Form, obtains OHCQ's written approval before operating, and guarantees awake overnight staffing and training resources.
Screens and assesses residents, writes service plans, schedules and tracks staff training and supervises unit care.
Assesses residents with cognitive impairment, reviews behavior plans and trains staff in resident-specific care.
Provide person-centered care, report behaviors and changes, and complete required training.

documentation: Alzheimer's Special Care Unit Disclosure Form and proof of submission
OHCQ written approval
Admission screening and Resident Assessment Tool
Service plan addressing behaviors
Care notes on behaviors and interventions
Staffing plan and dated schedules showing awake overnight staff (18 months)
Training log and certificates in personnel files
QA reviews of unit incidents

policies.title: Falls Prevention
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Assisted Living Manager, the delegating nurse and the Administrator.
policies.purpose: To reduce the number and severity of resident falls by identifying risk, planning prevention in the service plan, responding to every fall and tracking trends, in accordance with COMAR 10.07.14.28, 10.07.14.33 and 10.07.14.38.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] identifies each resident's fall risk at admission and whenever the resident's condition changes. The service plan addresses fall risk with specific interventions (COMAR 10.07.14.28). Staff complete an incident report within 24 hours of knowledge of any fall (COMAR 10.07.14.33). Bed rails and other protective devices may be restraints under COMAR 10.07.14.38 and are used only as stated in SAF-04. The delegating nurse reviews fall trends in the Quality Assurance process (GOV-04).

definitions.definition: Any unplanned event in which a resident ends up on the floor or ground or another lower surface, whether or not injury results, including when found on the floor.
A device as defined in COMAR 10.07.14.02 that is used for safety, such as a bed rail. Depending on how it is used, it may be a restraint (SAF-04).
An event as defined in COMAR 10.07.14.02. A fall is an incident.
The written plan of services based on the Resident Assessment Tool and nursing assessment, as required by COMAR 10.07.14.28.

procedures: Admission risk screen: At the pre-admission and admission assessment (ADM-01, ADM-03), the Assisted Living Manager (ALM) and delegating nurse record fall history, gait and balance, vision, footwear, continence, cognition, mobility aids and the use of medications that increase fall risk.

Service plan: The service plan, completed within 30 calendar days of admission, lists the resident's fall-risk level and specific interventions. These may include assistance with transfers and walking, a scheduled toileting plan, assistive devices, night lighting, nonslip footwear, and room arrangement (ADM-04).
Medication review: The delegating nurse and pharmacist look for medications that increase fall risk at the regimen review and every 45-day visit, and ask the practitioner to review them (HLT-02).
Environment: Staff keep walkways clear, spills cleaned, floors dry, lighting adequate, and call devices within reach. Housekeeping and maintenance report hazards to the ALM the same day (DL-03).

Daily practice: Staff follow the service plan, answer call devices promptly, offer toileting regularly, make sure walkers and canes are in reach, and watch residents at higher risk during meals and activities.

Response to a fall: Staff stay with the resident and do not move the person until checked. They call 911 for a suspected serious injury, head injury on a person taking blood thinners, or any sign of a serious condition. Otherwise they call the delegating nurse at [PHONE] right away.
Nurse assessment: The delegating nurse directs the post-fall check and any follow-up monitoring. Staff record vital signs, pain, injuries and neurological signs as directed.
Notifications: The ALM notifies the resident representative and practitioner as directed by the nurse, and records the times and persons notified (HLT-04).

Incident report: The staff member who witnessed or discovered the fall completes an incident report within 24 hours of knowledge, covering the circumstances, injuries, notifications and actions. The ALM reviews the report the same or next business day. Reports are kept on the premises and made available to OHCQ.

State reporting: If a fall results in a resident's death, the Administrator notifies OHCQ within 24 hours, as the rules require for a death resulting from an injury incurred at the program (SAF-02, REC-03).

Post-fall review: The ALM and nurse review each fall within 3 business days, find likely causes, and revise the service plan. Where a significant change has occurred, a full reassessment is done within 48 hours (HLT-04).

Bed rails and protective devices: Staff do not install or use bed rails, lap trays, belts or other devices to prevent falls unless the nurse has assessed the resident and a physician's order exists. The device is then treated as a possible restraint under SAF-04, including physician order, repositioning, family notification and 7-day renewal. Alternatives such as low beds, floor mats and scheduled checks are tried first.
Staff training: The delegating nurse trains staff at orientation and annually on safe transfers, fall response and risk reduction (STF-03).
Trend tracking: The ALM keeps a fall log with date, time, location, circumstances and injury. The ALM presents it to the delegating nurse monthly.

QA review: The delegating nurse reviews fall trends at least every 6 months at the ALM and RN meeting, identifies patterns by time, place or resident, and reports them in the QA plan with actions taken (GOV-04, HLT-03).

responsibilities.duty: Follow fall interventions, respond to falls and complete incident reports within 24 hours.
Assesses risk, updates service plans, notifies representatives and practitioners, keeps the fall log and reviews each fall.
Directs post-fall assessment, reviews medications, trains staff and reviews fall trends in QA.
Makes sure reports are made to OHCQ when required and resources are provided to correct hazards.

Service plan with fall interventions
Incident reports for falls (within 24 hours)

Fall log

policies.title: Skin Integrity and Pressure Injury Prevention
policies.applies_to: All direct care staff, the Assisted Living Manager, the delegating nurse and the Administrator.
policies.purpose: To prevent pressure injuries and other skin breakdown, detect them early, and make sure [AGENCY NAME] does not admit or keep residents whose skin condition exceeds what it may serve, in accordance with COMAR 10.07.14.28, 10.07.14.23 and 10.07.14.38.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assesses skin risk at admission and reassesses whenever condition changes. The service plan addresses pressure ulcers (COMAR 10.07.14.28). Staff report any skin change to the delegating nurse promptly. [AGENCY NAME] does not admit or retain a resident who needs treatment of a stage 3 or stage 4 pressure ulcer (COMAR 10.07.14.23 §B); see ADM-05. Any resident under a restraint is repositioned at least every 2 hours (COMAR 10.07.14.38).

definitions.definition: Localized damage to skin and underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence, caused by pressure or friction. It is staged from 1 to 4 by severity.
A deep ulcer involving full-thickness skin loss (stage 3) or exposed muscle, tendon or bone (stage 4). Treatment of these is outside what [AGENCY NAME] may admit or retain.
A physical, mechanical or chemical means that restricts a resident's movement, as governed by COMAR 10.07.14.38 and SAF-04. A protective device, such as a bed rail, may be a restraint.
The State-required assessment instrument defined in COMAR 10.07.14.02.

procedures: Pre-admission screen: Before admission, the Assisted Living Manager (ALM) and delegating nurse ask about current wounds, history of pressure injury, mobility and continence, and look at the skin when feasible (ADM-01). They record findings.

Stage 3 or 4 ulcer: If the applicant needs treatment for a stage 3 or 4 pressure ulcer, [AGENCY NAME] does not admit the person (COMAR 10.07.14.23 §B). The ALM gives the applicant and referral source the reason in writing and suggests other options. Hospice cases are handled under the hospice exception in COMAR 10.07.14.23 §D, and the ALM must confirm with the delegating nurse and ADM-05 before acting.

Admission skin check: A trained staff member, under the delegating nurse's direction, checks the resident's skin head to toe within 24 hours of admission with privacy and respect. Findings are recorded in the record.

Risk assessment: The ALM and delegating nurse include skin risk in the Resident Assessment Tool and nursing assessment. They look at immobility, incontinence, poor nutrition or hydration, diabetes, circulation problems and prior ulcers.

Service plan: The service plan, completed within 30 calendar days of admission, addresses pressure ulcer prevention. It names interventions such as turning and repositioning schedules, pressure-relieving cushions or mattresses, heel protection, incontinence care, nutrition and fluids, and skin checks (ADM-04).

Daily care: Staff check skin during bathing and dressing, keep the skin clean and dry, use moisturizers as directed, prevent friction during transfers, encourage walking or position change, and keep bedding and clothing smooth.

Nutrition and fluids: Staff encourage meals and drinks. The dietary staff report poor intake to the ALM, who tells the delegating nurse and arranges therapeutic diets or supplements if ordered (DL-01).

Report skin changes: Any staff member who sees redness that does not fade, blisters, broken skin, open areas, new bruising, drainage or odor reports it to the ALM and delegating nurse the same shift. Staff do not apply any treatment without an order.

Nurse assessment: The delegating nurse assesses the skin change, determines the stage, and issues a nursing order. The nurse contacts the practitioner as needed. The nurse documents the location, size, appearance and any orders (HLT-03).
Notify: The ALM notifies the resident's representative and, as directed, the practitioner, and documents it (HLT-04).
Reassessment: A new or worsening pressure injury may be a significant change. The ALM completes a full reassessment within 48 hours when it is, and revises the service plan (ADM-03, ADM-04).

Treatment limits: Staff apply only treatments ordered by the practitioner and delegated by the nurse within the program's scope. A resident with a stage 3 or 4 ulcer needing treatment is not retained. The ALM and Administrator begin the transfer or discharge planning under ADM-05, ADM-07 and ADM-08, with the proper notice and documentation.

Restraints: If a resident is under a physician-ordered restraint, staff reposition and toilet the resident at least every 2 hours and record each time (SAF-04). They check skin under and around the restraint at each repositioning and report any redness or breakdown to the nurse at once.
Documentation: Staff record skin checks, repositioning and reported changes in care notes, with at least weekly notes for every resident (REC-02).

Training and QA: The delegating nurse trains staff on skin checks and repositioning at orientation and annually (STF-03). The nurse reviews skin injuries in the QA process and corrects any gaps (GOV-04).

Assesses and stages skin changes, issues nursing orders, contacts practitioners, trains staff and reviews trends.
Makes sure the program does not admit or retain residents requiring treatment of stage 3 or 4 ulcers, and provides equipment and staff.
